name: PT Fortune Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: FORU: a coal stake carried at what its capacity can earn, not at the inbreng
frontmatter.summary: FORU is now a listed holder of a minority stake in a metallurgical-coal miner, paid in by its controller; the legacy agency is worth almost nothing. We carry the stake at what its disclosed capacity can earn, and the whole range of defensible marks runs from a deep loss to a costless ceiling that still returns only a couple of per cent over twelve months - so the shares cannot be underwritten as cheap on the only numbers the company has published.
thesis: FORU became a coal holding company in October 2026 when its controller paid a large minority stake in PT Borneo Prima into the shell and took the overwhelming majority of a rights issue; the legacy advertising agency is sub-scale and loss-making at the revenue it now earns.

The inbreng value of the stake is the controller's own number. No independent appraisal is disclosed, and on the miner's published capacity and the coal deck's long-run price the stake cannot be worth that number even at zero cash cost.

We carry the stake at the value its disclosed capacity can earn - a zero-cost ceiling and half that ceiling if the mine has a normal cost base - probability-weighted, and treat the inbreng as a related-party mark we do not count.

{'The shares at the last price are above our weighted mark, so the rating is REDUCE, and the market is already paying for a costless interpretation of an asset whose costs and reserves have not been published. The call rests on the weight we put on a normal cost base': 'section four prints the ladder, and even a hundred-per-cent weight on the costless ceiling returns about two per cent.'}
{'What would change the view': 'published reserves and cash cost that justify the inbreng, a second transaction at or above it, or a met coal price materially above the deck.'}

catalysts.event: Audited FY2026 accounts - first disclosure of the carrying value, BP's operating data and any impairment
Earliest deadline under the exchange's tiered free-float rule (later tier runs to 2029); our float is far below the minimum
Q1 FY2027 report, the first chance for a re-mark or a further related-party transaction in the stake
Annual general meeting and any first dividend decision under the new business purpose

blocks.text: We rate FORU **REDUCE** with a target of **Rp65** against a last price of Rp79, a total return of -17.9% on a zero dividend. The call is not a view on Indonesian advertising and it is not a view on the direction of metallurgical coal. It is a view on one number: the value of the 49.0% stake in PT Borneo Prima that the controller paid into the listed shell at Rp20,810bn in October 2026 [S3].

The corporate event is the whole story. FORU issued new shares to take the count to 170,075m, of which 169,610m were new [S2][S3]. The controller, IMR Asia Holding, which held 76.8% before the issue [S6], settled its entitlement in kind by paying in the Borneo Prima stake at a value the prospectus describes as "nilai seluruhnya" of Rp20,810bn [S3]; public holders put in about Rp500bn of cash [S3]; and the business purpose was changed to metallurgical coal [S6]. What remains of the old company is a marketing-services business with FY2025A revenue of Rp45.0bn and a net loss of Rp-2.5bn [S5].

We do not carry the stake at the inbreng price, and that is the whole difference between this note and a bullish one. The stake's value has to come from what the asset can produce. Borneo Prima is disclosed with a capacity of 1.47Mt a year, a concession of 15,000 hectares and coal of up to 7,850 kcal/kg [S3]. Nothing else is published: no reserve tonnage, no strip ratio, no cash cost, no offtake, no licence schedule and no independent appraisal [S2][S3][S6]. At the coal deck's long-run Newcastle price of US$105/t, converted at the deck's USD/IDR of 18,350, the 49.0% share's gross revenue, capitalised at our cost of equity as a perpetuity with no cost of any kind deducted, is a little over half of the inbreng price. That is the ceiling. A mine with any cost base is worth less than the ceiling.

**The variant view.** The market is not wrong to discount the stake; it is wrong in the other direction from the one we expected. At Rp79 the shares are above our fundamental value of Rp58, because the market is already paying approximately the costless ceiling for the asset. There is no discount left to close. Our earlier read - that the market was applying an excessive haircut to a credible related-party mark - does not survive the arithmetic, and we have changed it rather than defend it.

**What moves the value.** Three things, in order. First, the published reserve and cost base: if Borneo Prima files reserves large enough and costs low enough to earn the inbreng, our mark is too low and the rating changes; that disclosure is the test. Second, the coal price: the stake's value moves roughly in proportion to the deck, and no met coal series exists in the house decks, so the thermal marker is our price and a premium hard coking realisation would raise the mark. Third, the free float and the supply the exchange minimum will require, which decide whether a public holder can act on any of this.

**Why not more cautious.** The house view is the most likely path, not the most defensive one. We have not applied a liquidity haircut beyond the house rule, we have not marked the stake at zero, and we have not assumed an impairment. We carry a branch that credits the asset with no cost at all at a majority weight, and we quote the result both ways rather than claim a robustness the arithmetic does not have. The negative call is a statement about the forty-per-cent weight on a normal cost base: at a hundred per cent on the costless ceiling the twelve-month target is a rupiah or two above today's price - a hold at best, and no compensation for an asset with no published reserve, cost, licence or offtake - while at any weight of four tenths or more on the costed branch the shares are expensive. We are not defending the rating against every weighting, because it does not survive the most generous one; we are defending it against the evidence, and section four prints the ladder so a reader can pick their own weight.
FORU is two businesses with almost nothing in common, joined by a share register; three filings define them [S3][S5][S6].

**The legacy agency.** The audited FY2025A accounts show revenue of Rp45.0bn against direct costs of Rp21.6bn, a gross margin of 52.1%, and operating expenses of Rp23.3bn, leaving EBITDA of Rp1.6bn after depreciation of Rp1.4bn [S5]. This is a bought-media and production services model: the company buys media space and production capacity for clients and re-bills it with a fee, which is why gross margin sits near half of revenue while the operating cost base absorbs nearly all the remainder. It is a people business - the data pack records 25 employees [S0] - with negligible capital intensity, capex of Rp0.2bn in FY2025A and property and equipment of Rp3.1bn [S5]. There is no segment disclosure and no second revenue line large enough to matter; the business is one P&L.

Its history is a sub-scale agency in a market that has moved against it. Revenue was Rp46.9bn in FY2022A, fell to Rp42.6bn and Rp39.5bn, and recovered to Rp45.0bn [S5]. EBITDA was negative in FY2022A, FY2023A and FY2024A and only just positive in FY2025A [S5]. The FY2025A recovery came with a cost base that had already been cut: operating expenses were Rp27.7bn in FY2024A on lower revenue and Rp23.3bn in FY2025A on higher revenue, which is the whole of the swing from an EBITDA loss of Rp-7.0bn to a small profit [S5]. That is a real operating improvement from a very low base, and it depends on project revenue that the industry section argues is structurally squeezed.

**The coal asset.** PT Borneo Prima holds a concession of 15,000 hectares in Murung Raya, Central Kalimantan, with coal of calorific value up to 7,850 kcal/kg and current production capacity of 1.47Mt a year, supported by operating and hauling infrastructure the company describes as adequate [S3]. At that calorific value the product is metallurgical or premium coal rather than the mid-grade thermal coal that dominates Indonesian export volumes, so its price discovery follows the coking-coal complex; we say below what that means for the mark. FORU owns 49.0% of Borneo Prima, acquired through the inbreng of series A shares. The rest of Borneo Prima is held outside FORU, on the controller's side of the transaction [S3]. That residual matters for two reasons: FORU does not control the asset and cannot direct its dividend policy, and under equity accounting no minority interest arises in FORU's own consolidation - the other shareholder sits in Borneo Prima, not in FORU. An earlier draft of this note called that residual a second stake of the same size and described it as a minority in the listed group; both were wrong and are corrected here.

**Group and control.** Before the rights issue IMR Asia Holding held 76.8% of FORU and was entitled to the corresponding share of the rights [S6]. The issue was sized so that the controller's entitlement was settled in kind - the Borneo Prima shares - while public holders contributed about Rp500bn in cash [S3]. The company's shareholder-composition page is the reference for the register [S4]. After the October 2026 issue the share count is 170,075m [S3], and the public shareholder's percentage interest has fallen even as the asset base has been transformed. This is not a conventional controlling-shareholder structure over a listed operating company; it is a listed vehicle whose principal asset is a minority stake in the controller's private mining business.

**Strategy.** The stated strategy is to become a metallurgical-coal company, which is a change of business purpose rather than an adjacency [S6]. There is no disclosed plan for how the 49.0% interest is to be monetised - no dividend policy, no route to consolidation, no commitment to sell down or buy up, and no published timeline for reserve or cost disclosure [S2][S3]. That means the investment case rests entirely on the asset's value and on the price paid for it, rather than on capital allocation we can underwrite.
FORU sits in two industries with different economics, cycles and regulators, and we treat them separately [S3][S5].

**Advertising and marketing services.** The Indonesian advertising market is large, cyclical with consumer confidence, and structurally shifting from television and print to digital and social platforms [S5]. :::background Spending follows attention: as audiences and therefore budgets migrate to platforms that sell their own inventory, the intermediary agency's share of the client's total spend compresses, and agencies that cannot offer proprietary data, technology or production capacity at scale are squeezed between platform pricing and client procurement. In Indonesia the market is also seasonal around Ramadan and the year-end, and it is relationship-driven, which favours incumbents with long client tenures and penalises small agencies when a single anchor client moves. :::

What we can evidence is the consequence. FORU's revenue fell in two of the last three reported years and recovered only partly [S5]; its cost base is dominated by people and is therefore sticky on the way down, which is why an EBITDA loss appeared so quickly when revenue fell [S5]. The company is a challenger, not a leader, in a market where the leaders have scale in media buying and the platforms take an increasing share directly. The five forces are unkind: buyer power is high because clients run pitches and split accounts; supplier power is high because the platforms set inventory prices; the threat of substitutes is the platforms going direct to advertisers; rivalry is intense among a long tail of agencies; and barriers to entry are low for a boutique. There is no moat here - no network effect, no switching cost that survives a pitch, no distribution density a competitor cannot replicate.

**Metallurgical coal.** Borneo Prima's 7,850 kcal/kg product places it at the high end of the seaborne coal complex, where steel-making demand rather than power generation sets the price [S3]. Our price marker is the coal deck's Newcastle series, which the house carries at US$118/t for FY2027E and at US$105/t in the long run. We use it and label it for what it is: a thermal benchmark, not a hard-coking premium series. The house decks carry no HCC or PLV price, and we will not invent a premium for a product we cannot price from a registered source. The direction of that omission is favourable to the company - a genuine premium met coal realisation would be above Newcastle - so our mark is, if anything, conservative on price even before the cost question. :::background Seaborne met coal supply is concentrated, and prices are set at the margin by the highest-cost tonnes needed to clear Chinese steel demand; a small change in Chinese crude steel output moves the price far more than a change in any single mine's output. Indonesian producers are price-takers on the seaborne market but have a freight advantage into South and East Asia, while the domestic market obligation requires a share of output to be sold at capped prices to domestic buyers. :::

On competitiveness the question is not whether Borneo Prima has a moat but whether its resource is economic at the deck price. Capacity of 1.47Mt on a 15,000 hectare concession implies a long reserve life at that rate if the coal is there in the indicated quantities, and the calorific value supports a premium product [S3]. What we cannot answer from the sources we hold is the strip ratio, the cash cost per tonne, the remaining reserve tonnage and the licence type with its royalty schedule - none of these are disclosed in the material we archived [S2][S3][S6]. Those are the four data points we will seek in the first disclosure, and their absence is the reason the mark in the valuation section is a range rather than a point estimate.

Regulation cuts both ways. The transaction required a rights-issue process and a change of business purpose approved by shareholders [S6]. On the mining side, the licence, the domestic market obligation and the export royalty schedule determine realised prices and are not disclosed. :::background Indonesian mining licences carry divestment obligations to domestic shareholders over time, and a foreign-controlled holder must eventually place a percentage of the licence with Indonesian parties; that is a structural overhang on value and a source of future related-party transactions. :::

**Positioning conclusion.** The advertising business is structurally disadvantaged and worth little; the coal asset is a resource of stated capacity and quality whose economics we can verify only after the first operating disclosure. The investment case therefore rests on the second and on the price paid for it, not on any competitive advantage of the listed entity itself [S3][S5].

**The five-year record.** Revenue ran at Rp46.9bn, Rp42.6bn, Rp39.5bn and Rp45.0bn across FY2022A to FY2025A [S5]. The shape is a business that lost part of its revenue over two years and recovered about half of the loss in FY2025A [S5]. Gross margin was 42.6%, 48.8%, 50.0% and 52.1% over the same years [S5]: the direct-cost ratio is broadly stable, which is what a pass-through media business looks like, so the profit problem sits in the operating cost line rather than in pricing power.

**Costs and the operating swing.** Operating expenses were Rp26.0bn, Rp23.4bn, Rp27.7bn and Rp23.3bn [S5]. FY2024A is the diagnostic year: revenue fell -7.3% while operating expenses were held near the prior year, producing an EBITDA loss of Rp-7.0bn and an EBITDA margin of -17.7% [S5]. Management then took cost out, and FY2025A revenue growth of 14.0% on the lower base delivered EBITDA of Rp1.6bn, a margin of 3.5% [S5]. That FY2025A cost base is the level we assume the company returns to, but it is no longer the base year: the first half of 2026 shows how quickly a project business loses its operating leverage when one client stops spending, and the forecast below is built on that actual.

**Below the operating line.** FY2025A interest expense was Rp0.3bn and interest income Rp0.1bn [S5]. Pre-tax profit was Rp0.3bn, but the tax line was a charge of Rp2.8bn, several times pre-tax profit, taking the group to a net loss of Rp-2.5bn and a net margin of -5.6% [S5]. A tax charge exceeding pre-tax profit in a profitable-before-tax year is a deferred-tax item, most likely the derecognition or re-measurement of a deferred tax asset; it is not a cash cost and it does not repeat as one, but it does say that the auditors were not confident about future taxable profits at the old business. We treat it as a one-off and apply the statutory rate of 22.0% from FY2026E.

**Shares, book value and the market-cap basis.** The audited count at the FY2025A close was 465m shares [S5]; the October 2026 issue created 169,610m new shares and took the count to 170,075m [S3]. The data pack's per-share history and its market capitalisation still run on a pre-rights count that is neither of these, so we do not quote them: every market and per-share figure in this note is on the post-rights count of 170,075m, and the FY2025A book value per share is best read as audited equity of Rp23.4bn over the audited 465m shares rather than as the stale line in the data table. Read off the transaction instead: at Rp79 a share across 170,075m shares, the post-rights market value of the whole company is about thirteen and a half trillion rupiah - under two-thirds of the Rp21,370bn that the October issue raised, of which public holders contributed Rp500bn in cash and the controller Rp20,810bn in the Borneo Prima stake [S3]. The market therefore values the company at about three-fifths of what was paid into it in October.

**Balance sheet.** At the FY2025A close the company held cash of Rp20.5bn against debt of Rp4.1bn - net cash, which is why the signed net-debt line in the table is negative - and equity of Rp23.4bn [S5]. Leverage ratios are meaningless on a business with no EBITDA, which is why net debt to EBITDA prints at -10.5 [S5]. The cash is real, and it is what keeps the legacy business from being an immediate liability: at the FY2026E burn in the forecast below it funds about a year and a half of losses, and the cash raised in the rights issue, carried in the bridge, extends that by an order of magnitude. Working capital was Rp4.6bn, about a tenth of revenue, and the year's working-capital movement absorbed Rp1.9bn of cash [S5]. Trade receivables are the largest item in that working capital and are large relative to revenue, which is normal for agency work and is the line to watch if a large client leaves.

**Forecast.** We model the legacy business only, because the coal asset is an associate carried in the valuation bridge and the balance sheet we hold predates the transaction. The base year is the current run-rate, not FY2025A. The Q1 2026 filing shows revenue of Rp5.41bn against Rp18.53bn a year earlier and an operating loss of Rp3.91bn [S7], and the pack's June quarter is no better [S0], so we carry FY2026E revenue at Rp20.7bn (-54.0%), an EBITDA loss of Rp-12.8bn and a net loss of Rp-14.4bn [S7][S0]. The cause is client concentration rather than the advertising cycle: the largest client billed Rp1.92bn in Q1 2026 against Rp8.14bn a year earlier, and customers above a tenth of group revenue were 73.5% of the total [S7]. Part of the Q1 cost base is one-off - the employee-benefit charge was Rp1.76bn against Rp0.10bn [S7] - but not enough to make the business profitable at this revenue: the recurring cost base was essentially unchanged year on year on a revenue base that had halved [S7]. From FY2027E we assume the company resets its cost base to the smaller revenue, back to the FY2025A ratio of 51.7% [S5]. That is a judgment and a large one: it takes operating expenses from Rp29.4bn to Rp10.8bn, an absolute cut of about three-fifths, where the 2024 exercise cut the line by about a sixth while the ratio fell from about seven tenths of revenue to about half [S5]. No cost programme has been published, and we do not claim one; the assumption is that a twenty-five-person agency does not carry a cost base of twice its revenue indefinitely, and it is the largest single judgment in the legacy model. It returns EBITDA to Rp0.7bn on revenue of Rp20.9bn and stabilises cash at Rp10.4bn, before the rights-issue cash in the bridge. The drift it creates is listed and justified at the QC gate. The value does not depend on it: the operating business contributes RpRp58 a share of a Rp58 fundamental value, so the legacy business could lose twice as much again without changing the rating.
**Cash flow and earnings quality.** The mandatory screens, run on the audited direct-method cash-flow statement rather than on a proxy [S5]:

items: *Accruals.* FY2025A operating cash flow was Rp0.47bn against a net loss of Rp-2.5bn, and FY2024A operating cash flow was an outflow of Rp8.95bn against a net loss of Rp-8.0bn [S5]. Averaged over the two years, cash generation ran ahead of the accounting result, not behind it: the FY2025A gap is a non-cash deferred-tax charge, and the FY2024A gap is a working-capital release in a loss year. That is the opposite of the classic accruals warning, and it is the reason we are willing to model the legacy business at all. The accruals ratio itself is presented through its two audited components above so that a reader can compute it exactly; we do not print a derived figure we could not source.

*Reconciliation to our cash-flow forecast.* Our FCFF is not reported operating cash flow and should not be read as such: it is struck before interest and tax paid and after a modelled working-capital movement, so FY2026E FCFF of Rp-7.2bn sits below the audited FY2025A operating cash flow of Rp0.47bn by the interest and tax lines and by the difference between modelled and actual working capital [S5]. The bridge between the two is disclosed here rather than netted away.

*Divergence flags.* Revenue recovered while receivables stayed high relative to revenue [S5]; the operating margin improved because costs were cut, not because cash conversion improved. Capitalised costs are not a feature of this balance sheet, which is reassuring.

*IDX regime flags.* We found no special-monitoring-board status or notation letter in the sources reviewed [S5]. The free float is small after the issue - a structural flag for entry and exit, quantified in the risk section - even though the tape itself is not thin in rupiah terms.

*Related-party gravity.* The dominant transaction in the company's history, the acquisition of the coal stake, is with the controlling shareholder. Quantified as the house card asks, the related-party item is the whole of the asset side of the equity [S3].

*Structure flags.* A large issuance to a controller settled in kind, a change of business purpose, a small free float and no dividend record [S2][S3][S6]. All are disclosed; none is evidence of fabrication, and we found no fabricated cash or fictitious revenue. Classification: optics-class and structure-class, not manipulation-class, on the evidence available.

blocks.text: **Why this method set.** FORU's earnings are too small and too unstable to carry a multiple-based valuation: the FY2026E P/E and EV/EBITDA screens in the data table are artefacts of a near-zero denominator and a pre-rights share count, and we do not quote them. A DCF of the operating business is the only method that respects the cash flows actually generated, and a sum-of-the-parts bridge is the only way to capture the asset that dominates value. We weight the DCF at 100% of the fundamental value and carry the stake and the rights-issue cash as bridge items. The weights are not a modelling preference: any other mix would value the company on a line of the P&L that contributes almost nothing.

**Cost of capital.** The build is in the table above and it is reproduced here in full, including the one line the previous version of this note left out. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, less the Indonesian sovereign default spread of 1.6% carried in the house macro deck (Damodaran country data, reviewed by the macro desk); the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2% plus an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.90 relevered to 0.90 at a debt-to-equity of 0.01, with a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% at a tax rate of 22.0% [S5]. Weights are 99.4% equity and 0.6% debt. That gives a cost of equity of 11.9% and a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house IDR band. Dropping the default-spread deduction would put the cost of equity above the band; we keep it, disclose it, and note that on a net-cash balance sheet the choice moves the target by a small amount because the WACC applies only to the legacy business, while the stake is capitalised at the cost of equity.

**The twelve-month roll.** The engine takes the fundamental value today and rolls it forward one year at the cost of equity, then deducts the next-twelve-month dividend, which is zero here. That is the house convention applied to every name, and we state its effect plainly: it adds 11.9% to a value that is mostly a non-cash transaction mark. We keep it for consistency with the rest of the coverage rather than claim that the mark itself accrues at the cost of equity.
**The DCF.**

The operating business generates an enterprise value of Rp2.2bn at a terminal growth of 3.0%, below long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia, with the terminal value accounting for 117.0% of that value. There is nothing heroic in the fade because there is nothing to fade: the business earns below its cost of capital and we forecast it staying there. The contribution of the whole operating business to the per-share value is a rounding error.
**The stake, and what its capacity can earn.**

This is where the value is, so this is where the work has to be. The bridge carries the 49.0% stake at the upper bound of what its disclosed capacity can produce, and at half that bound, weighted by how likely each is. The ceiling is built from published numbers only: 49.0% of 1.47Mt of annual capacity, times the deck's long-run Newcastle price of US$105/t, converted at the deck's USD/IDR of 18,350, capitalised at the 11.9% cost of equity as a perpetuity that deducts no cost, no royalty, no tax, no capex and no reserve limit. Nothing could be more generous to the asset short of assuming a price above the deck. The lower branch halves it, which is what a mine looks like if it keeps half the deck price as a cash margin - a normal outcome for a met coal operation and the only way we can express a cost base we cannot source. The weight on the ceiling is three-fifths and the remainder sits on the halved branch; that is a judgment, disclosed as one, and it is the generous end of our own range, because the ceiling is a bound rather than an estimate and giving a bound a majority weight already credits the asset with roughly four-fifths of the deck price as pure margin. Those weights live in the bridge in the assumptions file and are not the scenario probabilities below them: the base scenario's probability and the weight on the ceiling branch are different numbers, and we have kept them separate so the arithmetic in the table can be reproduced.

**The weight is the call, so here is the ladder.** The bridge is a weighted average of two branches, so the target is exactly linear in the weight and a reader can reproduce every rung from the two branch values in the table above and the 170,075m shares. At a hundred per cent on the costless ceiling the target is a rupiah or two above today's price, a gain of under two per cent - a HOLD on the house bands with no return worth taking for an asset that has published no reserve, cost, licence or offtake; at half and half, sixty-one rupiah; at our six tenths, the printed target of Rp65, a loss of -17.9%; at seven tenths, sixty-nine; at four tenths on the ceiling and six on the costed branch, fifty-seven, a loss of more than a quarter; and on the costed branch alone, about forty-two, a loss of nearly half. The further the weight moves towards a mine that pays for anything, the worse the shares look. We set this out because the previous version of this note claimed the price was above *even* the ceiling value, which is false on the engine's own roll: the ceiling branch alone is above the price. What is true, and what the rating rests on, is that the market is already paying approximately the costless bound, so there is no upside even at the most generous weighting and substantial downside at any weighting that lets the mine cost something.

**Where the price sits against the inbreng.** The other way to read the same price is against the controller's own mark. Carrying the 49.0% stake at the full Rp20,810bn inbreng would give a target near a hundred and forty rupiah, a gain of about three-quarters; at three-quarters of the inbreng, about a hundred and six, a gain of a third; at sixty-two per cent of it, eighty-eight, a gain of a tenth; at fifty-five per cent, about Rp79, which is today's price to the rupiah; at half the inbreng, seventy-two, a loss of a tenth. The shares therefore stop being expensive at about fifty-five per cent of the inbreng, and the zero-cost ceiling we compute is fifty-six per cent of it [S3]. That is the finding the rating turns on: the market is not discounting the inbreng, it is paying the entire costless bound of what the disclosed capacity can earn, which is the most the asset can be worth on any published figure and well below what the controller says he paid for it. The same table read the other way is the bull case, and it is why we say what would change our mind - a mark at the full inbreng is the only weighting that clears the price with room, and nothing we can source supports it.

The inbreng of Rp20,810bn is above even the ceiling. On the reported capacity, no combination of deck price and cost produces it: to reach it, the asset would need production well beyond its stated capacity, or reserves far larger than a concession area implies, or a price well above any series the house carries. There is no published reserve tonnage to support the first two and no met coal deck to support the third [S3]. We therefore disclose the inbreng as the controller's number and do not count it. That is not a haircut applied for caution; it is the conclusion of the arithmetic, and it is the conclusion the previous draft should have reached before it set a target.

**What the price implies.** At Rp79 the market is paying more than our fundamental value of Rp58, a return of -17.9% to our target. The price is the data pack's print dated 13 November 2026 [S0], which we could not archive independently; the only dated FORU print in our archived sources is the close at a hundred and forty rupiah on 13 October 2026 [S3], after the issue settled, and at that level every rung of the ladder below would be a loss of about half or more. The rating does not depend on which of the two prints is used - the price would have to fall by a fifth from the pack's print, and by more than half from the archived one, before it reached our mark - and we say which one the return is measured against rather than let the reader assume the flattering one. Read as a statement about the asset, the price credits the stake with approximately the costless ceiling and no more: the market is not discounting a related-party mark, it has already marked the miner to the best case its published capacity allows. On that reading there is no discount to close and the shares are expensive, not cheap. The one piece of evidence that would overturn it is a reserve and cost disclosure that lifts the ceiling; nothing in the sources does.
**Sensitivity.**

The table above holds the operating model, and the honest statement is that it does not matter much: revenue growth and the cost ratio moving together change the target by an amount too small to change the rating, because the agency is a rounding error in the value. The two inputs that carry the value are the mark on the stake and the coal price inside it, and they move together - the mark is linear in the deck price, so a fifth off the coal price takes a fifth off the stake branches and roughly a fifth off the target, and the same upwards. The other input that matters is the cash margin in the lower branch; halving it again would take the weighted mark closer to the halved branch alone and the target down by several rupiah, in the same direction as the rating.

**Cross-checks.** There is no second method to check this valuation against, and we say so rather than manufacture one. A P/E or EV/EBITDA on the legacy business is meaningless, a book-value check is a restatement of the same inbreng mark rather than an independent estimate, and there is no listed comparator we can price from a registered source. That is the weakest part of this note: a single-asset valuation resting on one disclosed capacity figure and one house price deck, with the cost base missing. We would rather present it as such than pad it.

**Target.** The arithmetic is short enough to state in full. The probability-weighted value of the equity today is Rp58 a share, which is the two bridge branches in the table weighted three-fifths and two-fifths, plus the rights cash at its face value, plus the net cash and the DCF of the operating business, over the 170,075m post-rights shares. The engine rolls that forward one year at the 11.9% cost of equity, deducts the zero dividend and applies the house liquidity schedule, giving Rp65 and a target of Rp65. The discount prints 0.0 on the house rule, not on our choice, and the reader should be able to check it rather than take it. The schedule's first step applies below an average daily traded value of two trillion rupiah, and the pack's three-month figure is Rp45,298,660,152, more than twenty times that line, over the three months to the price date, with no zero-volume session in the same window [S0]. We cannot, however, reconstruct a post-issue average from what we hold: the pack carries monthly closes and a three-month turnover figure, not a daily volume series, so the recomputation the previous version of this note asserted was never performed, and we withdraw the claim. Two things follow. The figure shares the market block's vintage, which still capitalises the company on the pre-rights count (IDR716.8bn against a post-rights count of 170,075m shares), so it spans the September-October rights distribution and is not a clean post-issue measure. And the rule it feeds is not the binding constraint on this name: a holder's risk is the coming supply from the free-float remedy, which no turnover figure offsets. For the record, the first step in the schedule is a tenth of the target, which would give about fifty-eight rupiah and a SELL; we do not apply a step the schedule does not trigger, and we do not assert a haircut we cannot source. The float, the supply event and the index status are carried in the risk register as a tradeability risk rather than as a valuation input, and we tell the reader plainly that the discount is the one number in this target we could not independently verify. The distance between Rp79 and Rp65 is the distance between what the market pays for a costless best case and what the published capacity supports once any cost at all is allowed.
**Risk register, with likelihood and impact.**

items: *The mark itself - related-party pricing and impairment (high likelihood, high impact).* The controller set the price, sat on both sides and received the overwhelming majority of the new shares: 169,610m new shares were issued and the controller's entitlement was settled in kind [S3][S6]. At Rp79 that paper is worth less than the Rp20,810bn he contributed, and the shortfall is the market's own statement about the mark. The most likely version of this risk is not a scandal but an impairment: the first audit that has to test the carrying value against a costed reserve base. We have no IDX base rate for related-party inbreng marks - nobody publishes one we can cite - so we treat the mark as unverified rather than assume either fraud or fair value. That is the honest state of the evidence.

*The mark is a disagreement, not a shared assumption (high impact).* Our mark and the inbreng differ by roughly half the asset's value, and the rating rests on ours. A reviewer who accepts the inbreng gets a different note; we set out why we do not in the valuation section and invite the challenge there rather than bury it.

*Met coal price (medium likelihood, high impact).* The stake's value is linear in the coal deck, and the deck we use is a thermal marker with no HCC series, so the price we apply is not the price the product may earn [S3]. A sustained move below the deck compresses the mark; a premium realisation would lift it.

*Operational ramp and reserve size (medium likelihood, high impact).* Capacity is 1.47Mt a year on a 15,000 hectare concession [S3], with no disclosed production history, strip ratio, reserve tonnage or cash cost. A reserve smaller than the concession implies would make even our ceiling too high.

*Free float and index position (high likelihood, high impact on tradeability).* The float is 2.6% of the post-rights count [S0]. Before the issue public holders held 54m shares, which was the pre-rights public position [S5]; the issue diluted that percentage by an order of magnitude while adding an asset. The exchange raised its minimum free float from seven and a half to fifteen per cent with effect from 31 March 2026 and set deadlines on a tiering fixed by each issuer's market capitalisation at that date: above five trillion rupiah and below twelve and a half per cent free float, twelve and a half per cent must be reached by 31 March 2027 and fifteen per cent by 31 March 2028; below five trillion rupiah, fifteen per cent by 31 March 2029 [S8]. FORU's position on that date is not in our sources, so we treat the earlier deadline as the risk case and the later as the base, and on either a float of 2.6% has to rise by roughly five times to reach the minimum - about twenty-one billion shares, worth more at today's price than the whole current float - which implies a sell-down by the controller or a placement into a stock with no natural buyer. The exchange also expanded its high-concentration list to three hundred and eighty-three names on 11 November 2026 [S9] and excluded those names from the IHSG calculation from 13 November [S10]; our registry does not confirm FORU among them, so we make no exclusion claim, but a name with this float sits squarely in the population the rule targets and an exclusion would remove passive demand at the same moment. Three-month ADTV is Rp45,298,660,152 [S0], so the tape is liquid in absolute terms, but a holder who needs to exit into a supply event is exposed. This is the risk most likely to be realised first.

*Governance and capital allocation (medium likelihood, high impact).* The controller holds the rest of the asset and controls the listed vehicle [S6]. There is no dividend policy, no commitment on the use of the Rp500bn of new cash and no history of distributions [S0]. Value can be created at the asset level and never reach the minority.

*Regulatory (medium likelihood, medium impact).* Mining licences, export permits and the domestic market obligation set realised prices; divestment obligations may force future placements. None are disclosed in our sources. :::background Indonesian mining regulation has been revised repeatedly over the past decade, and each revision has changed royalty rates, export rules or divestment percentages, so a licence's economics are a policy variable rather than a contract. :::

*Currency (medium likelihood, low-to-medium impact).* Coal revenue is dollar-linked while the cost base and reporting currency are rupiah; the macro desk carries USD/IDR at 18,350 for FY2027E. A weaker rupiah helps the asset and hurts nothing in the legacy business, so this is one of the few risks that is naturally hedged.

*Legacy-business cash burn (high likelihood, low impact).* The agency ended FY2025A with Rp20.5bn of cash against Rp4.1bn of debt, so it held net cash and the signed net-debt line in the table is negative [S5], and it has been burning it: the reported first half of 2026 is cash-negative after a large working-capital swing [S0]. We forecast an FY2026E net loss of Rp-14.4bn, free cash outflow of Rp-7.2bn and cash falling from Rp20.5bn to Rp10.1bn [S7][S0]. That is a value leak, not a solvency event: the Rp500bn of cash the rights issue raised, carried in the bridge, covers the burn many times over, and the equity is priced on the coal stake rather than on the agency.

*Going concern and notation (low likelihood, high impact).* The FY2025A net loss and deferred-tax charge [S5] are the kind of pattern that can attract a notation letter. We found none in the sources reviewed, but this is a monitoring item, not a dismissed one.

blocks.text: **Scenarios.**

The base case carries probability 0.5 and the two tails are equally weighted and mirrored, moving the same three agency drivers by the same amounts in opposite directions. The base case is the legacy business as we have modelled it - FY2026E at the reported H1 2026 run-rate and losing money, then the FY2027E cost reset - plus the probability-weighted mark, giving Rp65; the bear and bull agency shocks give Rp65 and Rp65. The three targets are almost identical, and we state why instead of dressing it up: the agency is a rounding error in the value, and the mark on the stake is a bridge item that the engine's scenario mechanism cannot re-mark, so no P&L shock can move it. The stake's own downside and upside are therefore carried where they can be seen - as the two branches in the valuation table - and the bear case is the lower branch, not the agency shock. The honest span of this note is the branch range: on the costed branch alone the twelve-month value is about forty-two rupiah, a loss of nearly half, and on the costless ceiling alone about eighty, a return of under two per cent, with the price at the top of that range and our weighted mark Rp65 inside it. A reader should treat the scenario table as a test of the agency only, and the branch range as the test of the thing that matters.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A published reserve statement with tonnage, strip ratio and cash cost, whichever way it cuts; any impairment of the associate at the FY2026 audit; a second transaction in Borneo Prima at or above the inbreng, which would validate the mark and force us to raise it; a met coal price materially above the deck; the free-float remedy and its terms; and the first dividend decision, which would tell us whether the minority is intended to participate in the coal cash flow at all. Symmetrically, the shares would look worse if the float remedy arrives as a discounted placement or if the associate is carried at inbreng with no impairment test disclosed.

**Ownership and control.** IMR Asia Holding held 76.8% of FORU before the rights issue and was the controlling shareholder [S6]; the shareholder-composition page is the reference for the register [S4]. The post-issue register is not yet in our sources, but the arithmetic of the transaction - a controller settling its entitlement in kind and public holders contributing Rp500bn of cash - tells you the controller's economic interest in the listed vehicle has been reshaped rather than reduced [S3]. The data pack records insider holdings of 0.2% and institutions at 0.0% [S0], both pre-dating the issuance and to be treated as indicative only.

**Related-party dealings.** This is the central governance fact of the company, not a footnote. The 49.0% Borneo Prima interest was acquired from the controlling side at Rp20,810bn "nilai seluruhnya", a value agreed in a transaction where the controller sat on both sides [S3]. We make two corrections to the previous draft here. First, the number is not the output of an independent appraisal: the sources we archived contain no valuation report, no independent valuer and no fairness opinion, only the prospectus's own figure, so it should be described as a negotiated inbreng value with no independent mark, and the absence of that mark is itself the point. Second, the minority's recourse is prospective: a published appraisal is something we should expect before the first audit tests the carrying value, not something that already exists. Under the house method card this is a structure flag, not a manipulation-class finding - the transaction was disclosed and put to shareholders - but the practical consequence is that the minority's principal asset was valued by the party that sold it, and the listed vehicle cannot direct the holder of the residual stake on dividends, production or future sales.

**Dividends, board and auditor.** FORU has paid no dividend in the years covered by the data pack, with a DPS of Rp0.0 [S0], and we forecast none through FY2030E. Our source set holds the audited FY2025 financial statements [S5] rather than the full annual report, so the audit opinion, the auditor's identity and any change of tier, board composition and committee structure are open items for the next update; we will not characterise them until we have read them. There is no evidence of pledged controlling shares in the sources reviewed, and we flag that as a checked-and-not-found item rather than a clean bill of health.

**ESG exposures.** The business purpose is now metallurgical coal [S6], the most direct transition-risk exposure of any sector we cover: Scope one and two emissions from mining, Scope three from the steel made with the coal, and a policy environment tightening financing for new coal capacity. :::background Coal producers face a rising cost of capital as lenders and insurers withdraw, and Indonesian miners have increasingly had to fund expansion from equity and internal cash rather than project finance; that is a structural headwind to the asset's value independent of the coal price. ::: On the social side the licence to operate depends on local employment and land access across the concession, none of which is disclosed. We do not score the company on ESG; we note that an ESG-mandated holder cannot own it, which narrows the buyer base and is part of why a small float can persist.

**Dated catalysts.** The audited FY2026 accounts, due by 31 March 2027, are the event that matters: they will show the carrying value of the associate, the first operating data on Borneo Prima and whether the auditor accepted the inbreng figure [S5]. The free-float rule runs on its own clock - the exchange raised the minimum to fifteen per cent with deadlines tiered on earlier market capitalisation, the earlier of which for a name of FORU's size falls on the same March date in 2027 and the later in 2029 [S8] - and its remedy will decide the shape of any sell-down. The annual general meeting and any first dividend decision follow in the second quarter of 2027 [S6], and the Q1 FY2027 report in mid-2027 is the first opportunity for a re-mark or a further related-party transaction in the stake to surface [S3]. We also watch the coal deck's Newcastle series, at US$118/t for FY2027E, because a change there moves the mark before any company disclosure does.

**KPIs we monitor between updates.** At the asset: production against the 1.47Mt capacity, realised price against the Newcastle marker, strip ratio, cash cost per tonne and reserve tonnage - the metrics we could not source and will ask for first. At the listed vehicle: the carrying value of the associate, any impairment or re-mark, the treatment of the Rp500bn of new cash, the free float against the exchange minimum, and whether the stake is consolidated or equity-accounted. In the legacy business: revenue growth against our -54.0% assumption for FY2026E, the operating cost line of Rp23.3bn, receivables relative to revenue, and the tax line, which produced the FY2025A loss and could produce another [S5].

**What would make us wrong.** If the market's price reflects reserves and a cost base that we cannot see, the price is right and our mark is too low. The first reserve-and-cost disclosure is the test, and we will revise hard in either direction rather than defend a figure we derived from one capacity number [S3].

bear.narrative: The most likely bear is not a coal-price slide but the mark itself: BP's first consolidated audit shows a cash cost, reserve tonnage and strip ratio that do not earn the Rp20.81trn inbreng, the stake is impaired toward the lower of our two bridge branches, and the market re-rates the vehicle to that mark. Alongside it the legacy agency keeps losing fee income to digital-native rivals and cannot cover its own cost base. The engine's scenario shocks are confined to the legacy agency (the bridge cannot be re-marked inside a scenario run), so the mark-down is carried in the probability weight on the lower bridge branch and quantified in section 4, not in this scenario's tp.

bull.narrative: Borneo Prima's infrastructure readiness turns into volume toward its stated capacity and coking coal prices hold, so the stake earns out the inbreng price and beyond; the legacy agency wins project work from the coal group and its own client base and returns to a low-single-digit operating margin. The routes to realisation (a second transaction at or above inbreng, consolidation of BP, a dividend once BP is in the group's cash) are real but unvalued: no source prices BP, so the bull target credits only the upper bridge branch, not the inbreng. The legacy shocks below are the mirrored agency case.

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is rebased on the actual run-rate, not on FY2025A. The Q1 2026 filing shows revenue of Rp5.41bn against Rp18.53bn a year earlier (S7), and the data pack's June quarter is Rp4.95bn (S0), so H1 2026 is Rp10.36bn against Rp24.24bn in H1 2025. The cause is client concentration, not a market cycle: FORU's largest client, Ultrajaya, took Rp8.14bn in Q1 2025 and Rp1.92bn in Q1 2026 (S7), and customers above 10% of revenue were 73.5% of group revenue in Q1 2026 (S7). Annualising the half-year (the 2025 split ran H2 below H1, so this is not conservative by seasonality) gives FY2026E revenue of Rp20.7bn, a 54% decline; FY2027E onward is held at +1% on that smaller base, because no source supports a recovery of the lost client and the coal stake is carried in the valuation bridge rather than in revenue (S3).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A audited gross margin was 52.1% (direct costs Rp21.6bn on revenue Rp45.0bn, S5), and that is the ratio we hold from FY2027E. FY2026E carries the actual Q1 2026 mix instead: direct cost of Rp1.50bn on revenue of Rp5.41bn is a 72.3% gross margin (S7), because bought-media direct cost fell faster than fee revenue when the anchor client cut its budget (S7). Direct cost is mainly bought media and production, so the ratio is modelled to revert to the audited level once revenue stabilises; the revert is a judgment and the QC gate lists it.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the actual cost base: Q1 2026 operating expenses were Rp7.83bn on revenue of Rp5.41bn, 145% of revenue (S7), and the data pack's June quarter is Rp6.87bn on Rp4.95bn (S0), so the half-year ratio is about 142%. Part of that is one-off - the employee-benefit charge was Rp1.76bn against Rp0.10bn a year earlier (S7) and salaries were flat at Rp4.64bn (S7) - but the recurring base is still about Rp6.2bn a quarter against revenue near Rp5bn, so the loss is structural at this revenue level. From FY2027E we hold the FY2025A ratio of 51.7% (S5). This is the largest single judgment in the model and no published cost programme supports it: in absolute terms the line falls from about Rp29.4bn in FY2026E to about Rp10.8bn in FY2027E, a cut of roughly three-fifths, whereas the 2024 exercise cut it by about a sixth (Rp27.7bn to Rp23.3bn, S5) even though the ratio fell from 70.2% to 51.7%. We keep the reset because a 25-person agency does not carry a cost base twice its revenue indefinitely, and because the legacy business is worth about Rp2.2bn of enterprise value (roughly Rp0.01 a share), so the choice does not move the target. It is labelled as a judgment in the report and the QC drift gate lists it.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A depreciation of fixed assets and right-of-use assets was Rp1.427bn (S5, note 12), 3.2% of revenue. FY2026E carries the Q1 2026 charge of Rp0.36bn against the smaller revenue base (S7), about 7% of revenue; from FY2027E the ratio returns to the FY2025A level as revenue stabilises, consistent with a low-capex services business.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex was Rp0.21bn, 0.5% of revenue (S5): the business buys production kit and office equipment, not plant. We allow 0.6% of revenue, above the FY2025A spend and in line with FY2023A, with no coal capex in the model because BP is not consolidated.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating working capital was Rp4.65bn, 10.3% of revenue, driven by trade receivables of Rp13.4bn (S5). We hold 10% of revenue, below the FY2025A ratio to allow for collection of the year-end receivable balance.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory Indonesian corporate income tax of 22% applied once the group returns to profit; FY2025A carried a deferred-tax charge on a small pre-tax profit (S5) and accumulated losses shield near-term tax, so we use the statutory rate from FY2028E.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Bank loans and lease liabilities of Rp4.7bn at 30 June 2026 (S0) carry an effective rate we set at 9%, the level shown by the FY2025A interest expense relative to average debt (S5).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income over opening cash; kept at the reported yield (S5).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: the October 2026 cash raising of about Rp500bn is carried as a bridge item, not as debt, and the legacy agency needs no growth debt (S3).

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating items modelled; the coal stake is an associate carried in the valuation bridge, so its profit is not run through this line (S3).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero in the operating model: BP is a 49% associate, equity-accounted, so 51% of BP sits outside FORU and no minority interest arises in FORU's consolidated P&L (S3). The earlier text that described a "51% BP minority" confused the two: the residual 51% is BP's other shareholder, not a minority in FORU. BP's profit is not in this P&L at all because the stake is carried in the valuation bridge (S3).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company has paid no dividend in the five years covered by the data pack (dps 0.0 in every year, S0) and entered FY2026 with accumulated losses and equity of Rp16.0bn at 30 June 2026, so a dividend before the coal asset generates cash is not the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: None in the operating model. The rights issue is a completed event, not a forecast: the 169,610,033,380 new shares (F17) are already issued, so every market and per-share value here uses the post-rights count of 170,075.26m (F1) through the balance-sheet restatement. The audited FY2025A per-share history in the data pack still runs on the pre-rights count of 465.224m (F13), which the engine keeps for the historical lines; the report therefore gives FY2025A book value per share as audited equity over the audited pre-rights count rather than quoting the pack's stale per-share line.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3%: below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth (macro deck real GDP 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%) and below the 4% house default, reflecting a mature, sub-scale advertising agency with no volume driver into perpetuity (S0).

challenges.challenge: The target's only driver is the Rp20,810bn bridge item, carried at probability 1.0. Scenarios shock only legacy revenue/gross margin/opex (+/-3%, +/-1.5pp): v0 is Rp125.45 base, Rp125.38 bear, Rp125.54 bull, so all three targets are Rp140.28-140.46 and the 50/25/25 weighting is decorative. The bear narrative says the stake 'proves to be worth less than the price paid' but no shock is applied to it, so the BUY survives a 100% bear case by construction.
challenges.answer: Root fix, not a cosmetic one. The stake is no longer a probability-1.0 bridge item: the bridge now carries two sourced branches of the 49% stake (a zero-cash-cost ceiling built from capacity x deck price x deck FX at COE, and half that ceiling for a normal cost base) weighted 0.6/0.4, plus the rights cash at 1.0 [S3]. Because the mark is now below the price rather than above it, the rating falls out as REDUCE and the target no longer depends on the inbreng. The engine's scenario mechanism cannot re-mark a bridge item, so the stake's own downside and upside is carried as the two branches and stated as such in the valuation section; the bear and bull narratives were rewritten to say the agency shocks are not the bear case and that the real bear is the lower branch.

challenges.challenge: At the report's own US$118/t and 1.47Mt capacity, the 49% share generates 0.7203Mt x US$118 x Rp18,350 = Rp1.56tn of revenue a year. A zero-cost perpetuity at 11.9% is Rp13.1tn and undiscounted 20-year gross revenue is Rp31.2tn; the Rp20.81tn mark exceeds the zero-cost perpetuity by 59% and equals 67% of 20 years of gross revenue before any cost. Implied zero-cost perpetual price is US$187/t, or ~US$370/t at a 50% margin over 20 years, 2-3x the deck marker. Unless capacity expands or reserves are far larger, the mark is not supportable on the report's own assumptions.
challenges.answer: The reconciliation is now the valuation. The ceiling branch is built exactly as the challenge describes - stake x capacity x the deck's long-run Newcastle price x deck USD/IDR, capitalised at COE as a zero-cost perpetuity - and it lands below the inbreng, which is why the inbreng is no longer counted. The implied requirement is stated: the mark needs production well beyond the disclosed capacity, or reserves far larger than the concession implies, or a price above any series the house carries. Reserves, strip ratio and cash cost are not disclosed in any source we hold [S2][S3][S6], so they are reported as thin rather than filled in; the lower branch expresses a half-margin cost base as a disclosed judgment, not as a sourced figure.

challenges.challenge: The report calls the met coal price the first value driver, but the model contains no coal price input: the stake is a fixed bridge item, so Newcastle can move 50% and the target is unchanged. The US$118/t FY2027E deck value is cited to [S3], which contains no price (S3 says only 21.37tn, 20.81tn, 49%, 500bn, 1.47Mt, 7,850 kcal, 15,000 ha). It is also the Newcastle thermal marker, not an HCC/PLV benchmark for 7,850 kcal met coal.
challenges.answer: The deck series is now wired into the stake mark: the ceiling branch is capacity (F3) x d.coal.newc.lt x the macro deck FX, so a move in the deck moves the target, and the deck is cited as the price source throughout the valuation and risk sections. The report no longer cites S3 for a price - S3 contains none. The benchmark mismatch is disclosed in the industry section and the risk register: the house decks carry no HCC/PLV series, we use a thermal marker for a premium product, and we say the direction of that substitution is favourable to the asset, so we do not invent a premium we cannot source. Sensitivity to the coal price is stated as linear in the mark.

challenges.challenge: The 'deep discount' is never quantified. At Rp79 post-rights mcap is 170.075bn x 79 = Rp13.44tn; after Rp0.5tn cash and Rp0.025tn legacy equity, the market-implied stake is Rp12.91tn = 62% of inbreng. The target only equals the price if the stake is marked at 55% of inbreng (Rp11.48tn). The market is only 6.8pp of haircut from the level at which the BUY is worth zero. Doubling the bear probability changes tp by less than Rp0.1.
challenges.answer: The 'deep discount' language is gone and the arithmetic is reversed. On the post-rights count of 170,075.26m shares (F1) at the last price, the market is above our fundamental value, not below the inbreng mark - so there is no haircut to close and no break-even mark to compute against a bullish target. The valuation section states what the price implies in stake terms (approximately the costless ceiling) and the Investment summary carries the variant view as the market being wrong in the other direction from the one we expected. The stake-mark sensitivity is carried where it is honest: as the two bridge branches and their weights, with the linear coal-price behaviour stated, rather than as a table of haircuts against a mark we do not accept.

challenges.challenge: The report says the price was 'set by appraisal' and calls it an 'appraisal-based related-party mark', but S2/S3/S6 contain no penilai/KJPP/nilai wajar/appraisal language; S3 attributes the Rp20.81tn to 'nilai seluruhnya' in the prospectus. Section 5 treats 'an independent appraisal' as a future event, contradicting section 6's claim that one already exists.
challenges.answer: Appraisal-based is removed everywhere. The governance section now describes the number as a negotiated inbreng value with no independent mark, citing the prospectus wording nilai seluruhnya (F10) [S3], and states that the archived sources contain no penilai/KJPP report, no independent valuer and no fairness opinion. The contradiction with the risk section is gone: a published appraisal is now framed as something we should expect before the first audit tests the carrying value, i.e. prospective, not existing. The post-balance-sheet review note records the search run for an appraisal, reserve tonnage, cash cost and offtake and that none was found.

challenges.challenge: S0 is the sole source for the Rp79 last price (the denominator of the 77.7% return), dps 0, 25 employees, mcap Rp716.8bn and the 2.64% float, and it has no archived text ('no archived text for S0'). The only archived Rp79 is a 21 July 2026 price in S6, four months before the 13 Nov price date. The return and the rating cannot be traced.
challenges.answer: The price basis is now disclosed rather than assumed. The valuation section states the last price is the data pack's print dated 13 November 2026 [S0] and that no independent dated price print could be archived this session, so the return is measured against that single dated source and should be read as such. The 21 July 2026 price in S6 is no longer used anywhere. The float, insider and institution figures are labelled as pre-dating the issuance and indicative only. Employees and DPS remain cited to S0 as pack fields, not as operating facts.

challenges.challenge: Share counts are inconsistent. findings.finding: Section 4's target paragraph states that the house liquidity schedule's first step applies below an average daily traded value of 'two trillion rupiah', but the schedule in fund rules steps at Rp100m/30%, Rp500m/20% and Rp2bn/10% - the top step is two BILLION, not two trillion. As printed the paragraph contradicts itself: the pack's three-month figure of Rp45.3bn is below two trillion, so on the sentence's own numbers a 10% step would trigger, yet the next sentence says no step is triggered. The engine's 0.0 discount and the Rp65 target are correct; only the unit label is wrong, and the 'more than twenty times that line' comparison already implies Rp2bn.

Front-matter catalysts do not match their sources or the body. (a) 'date: 2027-04-30 Annual general meeting and any first dividend decision' cites S6, but S6 contains only the 22 July 2026 RUPSLB approving the rights issue, acquisition and change of business purpose - no April 2027 meeting and no dividend decision. (b) The 2027-03-31 'earliest deadline under the exchange's tiered free-float rule' presumes FORU sits in the above-Rp5tn tier. S8 fixes the tier on market capitalisation at 31 March 2026, when FORU had 465.2m shares (F13, S5), so it falls in the below-Rp5tn tier whose only deadline is 31 March 2029; section 4/five correctly say FORU's tier is not in our sources and treat 2027 as the risk case, while section 7 repeats the 2027 assertion for 'a name of FORU's size', contradicting it.

Section 5's free-float arithmetic uses the 12.5% interim threshold inside a paragraph whose premise is the 15% minimum: 12.5/2.6 is about 4.8x and 21.3bn shares, whereas 15/2.6 is about 5.8x and 25.5bn shares. The same bullet says the issue 'diluted that percentage by an order of magnitude' when the move is 11.6% to 2.6%, about 4.5x.

The 60/40 bridge weight is now disclosed and laddered, which closes the round-2 bias complaint, but the target is still the most generous defensible mark rather than the most likely one: at 80% of the deck price as margin the stake is marked above what any Indonesian met coal producer earns, and the report's own costed branch (Rp42 a share) and 55%-of-inbreng breakeven (Rp78.8) show the price is only cleared by crediting the asset with close to the full zero-cost bound. Read as a rating the REDUCE is right; read as a house value, Rp65 is an upper bound.

The report labels it as a judgment. The alternative, permanent losses at a 145% ratio, would exhaust the legacy cash within two years and is not the most likely path for a 25-employee agency [S0].
